newsitem.title: USA: Foreign crude offerings into U.S Gulf still sparse.
newsitem.headline: Foreign crude offerings into U.S Gulf still sparse.

text.p: Offerings of foreign crude into the U.S. Gulf Coast remained on the dry side amid a number of factors including a still-tight Brent/West Texas Intermediate arbitrage, traders said.

NYMEX meanwhile said foreign crude deliveries on its July contract amounted tp 805,000 barrels out of a total of 1.271 million barrels delivered -- a lower number than in recent months that reflects solid refiner buying.
Traders have also said the trend is petering out for the moment because the narrow WTI/Brent spread has eliminated the immediate incentive for bringing crude across the Atlantic.

Regarding the slowness in the foreign scene, players also cited the fact that August loading programs have not yet started in earnest, notably the one for Colombian Cusiana, which is likely to be bigger than ever before in August.

Additionally, OPEC's meeting in Vienna may be keeping some players from closing deals until they see how it turns out, with the same views applying to Tuesday inventory data from the American Petroleum Institute (API).
"I think it's all of the above," said one trader, referring to the reasons behind the lull in the market.

But the lack of offers, particularly of Latin American crudes, proved to be a boon for domestic sour grades, and underscored the claims of some traders that some refiners' July program requirements were not quite met, notwithstanding the lull in the action.
But the Cusiana loading program, set to be announced later this week, could jump start the bidding and offering in August.

Traders are expecting the size of the Cusiana August program to increase by anywhere from one to three cargoes as production volumes from the elephant field continue to grow. The program most rececently has been eight or nine cargoes.
Traders said the beginnings of August action were on display on the West African front, with two Angolan Cabinda cargoes for early arrival at the Gulf Coast heard offered.
